This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the [Backing Track](../../tools/backing-track.qmd) band plays: **Hymn: four parts**. It is built up from a simpler pattern, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read the band's last four bars on the staff underneath. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

[All the accompaniment patterns](index.qmd) · [Comping rhythms](index.qmd#chords)

## The pattern

Every chord played once and held until the next one. On the piano or organ it is four parts: the root in the left hand and three voices above it that move as little as possible from chord to chord. It follows the chart's chords, so a carol written with a chord on every beat sounds like the hymnal.

It belongs in *Hymn (four parts)*, *Folk carol* and *Piano ballad*. Here it is in the hymn (four parts) style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="hymn" data-chart="C|F|G|C" data-tempo="80" data-on="bass comp drums congas" data-staves="comp" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Comping rhythm:" data-choices='[{"label":"Hymn: four parts","opts":{"compRhythm":"hymn"}}]'></div>

## Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: [the lesson on it](chords-pad.qmd) takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="hymn" data-chart="C|F|G|C" data-tempo="56" data-on="comp drums" data-staves="comp" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Step:" data-choices='[{"label":"Long notes","opts":{"compRhythm":"pad"}}]'></div>

## Step 2: Hymn: four parts, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

**How to play it.** Four parts: left hand plays the root; right hand plays three notes that move as little as possible to the next chord. Keep any note two chords share in the same finger, and move the others to the nearest note of the new chord.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="hymn" data-chart="C|F|G|C" data-tempo="56" data-on="comp drums" data-staves="comp" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Compare:" data-choices='[{"label":"Hymn: four parts","opts":{"compRhythm":"hymn"}},{"label":"Long notes (the step before)","opts":{"compRhythm":"pad"}}]'></div>

## Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 80 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band's chord player off and take the part yourself.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="hymn" data-chart="C|F|G|C" data-tempo="80" data-on="bass comp drums congas" data-staves="comp bass" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Comping rhythm:" data-choices='[{"label":"Hymn: four parts","opts":{"compRhythm":"hymn"}}]'></div>

## Step 4: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="hymn" data-chart="C F|G C|Am F|G C" data-tempo="80" data-on="bass comp drums congas" data-staves="comp bass" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Comping rhythm:" data-choices='[{"label":"Hymn: four parts","opts":{"compRhythm":"hymn"}}]'></div>

## Step 5: In 3/4

The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="waltz" data-chart="C|C|F|F|G7|G7|C|C" data-tempo="120" data-on="bass comp drums congas" data-staves="comp" data-meter="3/4" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Comping rhythm:" data-choices='[{"label":"Hymn: four parts","opts":{"compRhythm":"hymn"}}]'></div>

## In other styles

The same comping rhythm in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.
